stories.headline: Arizona Holds Primary Elections With Governor, Key Congressional Seats at Stake
stories.summary:
Arizona voters headed to the polls Tuesday in an earlier-than-usual July primary, deciding nominees for governor, secretary of state, and several congressional races that could influence control of the U.S. House. State lawmakers moved the primary date from August to July earlier this year to allow more preparation time ahead of the November general election.

Republicans see a rare opportunity to unseat a first-term Democratic incumbent in what has historically been a red state. Six of Arizona's nine House seats are currently held by Republicans. Democratic contests have been complicated by internal party divisions over U.S. policy toward Gaza, adding an additional dimension to several races.

Arizona is considered a perennial battleground, and the outcomes of the governor's race and key statewide offices — including secretary of state, which oversees elections — carry national significance heading into the 2026 midterm cycle. Results are expected Tuesday night.

stories.headline: Army Veteran Arrested After Setting Fire, Firing Pellet Gun at Manhattan Federal Building Housing ICE
stories.summary:
Andrew Arrabaca, 43, a former U.S. Army soldier from Poughkeepsie, New York, was arrested Monday morning after setting fire to the entrance of 26 Federal Plaza in lower Manhattan, a federal building that houses ICE, the FBI, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services offices. Arrabaca allegedly poured accelerant on the building's stairs and ignited it, fired an airsoft pellet gun toward the building, and set off fireworks. He was armed with two axes, a machete, and three knives when federal agents tackled and detained him.

Three people sustained minor injuries, including two government employees and an immigrant who was present for a status hearing. FBI New York Assistant Director James Barnacle said Arrabaca "made several anti-government and anti-ICE statements during the incident" and described him as "an anti-American, anti-government extremist." The Department of Homeland Security referred to him as an "anti-ICE rioter."

Arrabaca served in the regular Army from 2001 to 2004 and in the New York Army National Guard from 2004 to 2005, reaching the rank of specialist with no overseas deployments. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the incident "deeply disturbing" and said his administration would hold accountable anyone who threatens public safety. The site has been a recurring flashpoint for protests against the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies.

stories.headline: Update: UK Borrowing Overshoots Forecasts as Burnham Government Faces Fiscal Pressure
stories.summary:
New data released Tuesday shows the United Kingdom borrowed more than forecast in the first three months of the fiscal year, delivering an early economic warning to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office Monday. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey now faces immediate pressure to manage the public finances while meeting the new government's spending commitments.

The borrowing overshoot underscores the fiscal constraints inherited by the Burnham government, which replaced the previous administration amid political turbulence. Healey, formerly defense secretary, will need to balance fiscal discipline against expectations for investment in public services that featured prominently in the Labour-aligned platform.

The figures add urgency to early budget decisions and could limit the new government's room to maneuver on tax and spending in its first months in office. Markets and analysts are watching for signals from Healey on how he intends to address the gap.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Agrees to Hear Asset Forfeiture Case Involving $95,000 Plane Seized Over a Six-Pack of Beer
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court agreed Monday to hear the case of Kenneth Jouppi, an 82-year-old Alaska man whose Cessna plane, valued at approximately $95,000, was confiscated by state authorities in 2012 after a single six-pack of beer was found aboard. Jouppi, who operated a one-man air taxi service, was flying a customer to the dry village of Beaver, Alaska, where local ordinance banned alcohol. He was convicted of a misdemeanor for alcohol importation, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld the seizure of his plane under the importation ban.

Jouppi has argued the forfeiture violates the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on excessive fines. The Supreme Court's decision to take the case gives the justices an opportunity to significantly constrain civil and criminal asset forfeiture practices by state and local governments, which collectively generate billions of dollars annually. The Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, filed a brief supporting Jouppi, arguing courts have strayed from the original understanding of the Eighth Amendment's protections.

Alaska maintains that confiscating aircraft used to facilitate illegal imports is a necessary enforcement tool. Civil liberties advocates on both the left and right have long criticized asset forfeiture as prone to abuse, while law enforcement agencies argue it is essential to disrupting criminal enterprises. The ruling, expected in the court's next term, could reshape how governments at all levels seize property connected to even minor offenses.
